items.title: How one nuclear blast could cripple nearly every satellite in low Earth orbit
items.desc: We rely on satellites every day for communications, weather forecasts and security, and more than 13,000 are currently circling the planet in low Earth orbit. But they could be more vulnerable than previously thought. Researchers have found that a single nuclear explosion in space could disable almost all of them.

items.title: Borneo forest survey reveals how mosquito abundance varies with river distance and height
items.desc: Several years ago, a researcher from Kyoto University was conducting fieldwork in Borneo in an effort to understand why certain primates frequently choose trees along rivers as sleeping sites. Among other potential hypotheses, he wondered whether there were fewer mosquitoes along riverbanks, allowing primates to sleep more comfortably. This question soon motivated him and his team of researchers to investigate how mosquito abundance varies between riverbanks and inland forests.

items.title: The carbon bubble question: How much are fossil-fuel companies really at risk?
items.desc: The global shift toward cleaner energy raises a difficult financial question: Are fossil-fuel companies worth more than they should be because investors have not fully accounted for the risks of climate change and stronger climate policies?

items.title: Quantum observers can 'agree to disagree,' but within limits, new theorem shows
items.desc: Two observers can start with the same description of a quantum system, follow the same probability rules and still disagree about the chance of the same outcome—even while being certain of each other's assessments.

items.title: Small life, big job: Enlisting microbes to fight climate change
items.desc: A working quarry isn't a pretty sight. Dust and bare rock, deep cuts into a hillside that appear like steps made for a giant. Nothing grows here, or so you would assume.

items.title: Astronomers track a flaring dwarf-star duo with exceptional precision
items.desc: Astronomers have measured the orbit, masses and distance of a pair of small, active stars with extraordinary precision, using the U.S. National Science Foundation's Very Long Baseline Array (NSF VLBA), operated by the U.S. National Science Foundation National Radio Astronomy Observatory (NSF NRAO). The observations provide a remarkably detailed picture of DG CVn, a binary system in which two red dwarf stars orbit each other about 59 light-years from Earth.

items.title: We know which young people are most likely to end up NEET in England—but not why
items.desc: In response to Alan Milburn's landmark review of England's NEET crisis—nearly 1 million young people ages 16–24 in the U.K. are not in education, employment or training—Prime Minister Andy Burnham has promised a "whole-childhood approach."

items.title: Liming soil could help protect crops during extreme heat waves
items.desc: New research has shown that liming soil to improve its pH buffering capacity could help plant roots survive heat waves and maintain crop productivity under high temperatures.

items.title: Building children's numeracy foundations involves more than 1, 2, 3
items.desc: As adults, we may take for granted what we know about numbers and how we arrived at this knowledge—for example, when comparing item prices to get the best deals or getting to appointments on time.

items.title: Pest mite overcomes catechin defenses in tea crops through a gene acquired from fungi
items.desc: Scientists have revealed how a major pest of tea crops can escape the tea plant's natural catechin defense mechanisms. The research, published in eLife provides convincing evidence that links an enzyme, DOG15, with the ability of a spider mite to adapt to and overcome the catechin-based defenses of tea.

items.title: Whom do we expect to put others ahead of themselves: Boys or girls? New study has surprising, and unsurprising, answers
items.desc: The holiday season is a time for gatherings with family and friends—as well as for less festive but necessary duties: organizing, preparing for and cleaning up after these gatherings. These are examples of service tasks that, according to previous research, women and girls are expected to perform.

items.title: Why punishment doesn't always prevent crime
items.desc: From "three-strikes" laws to longer prison sentences, harsher penalties are imposed in the hope they'll reduce crime. But decades of research show that increasing punishment often does surprisingly little. What if we're missing something crucial? New research from the University of California San Diego suggests one potentially overlooked reason: people's moral motivations for breaking the law in the first place.

items.title: This supernova is 50 million light-years away, but that's close enough for astronomers
items.desc: A new supernova has been spotted in NGC 1433, a spiral galaxy about 50 million light-years away. That's pretty close for supernova observations, and it's an opportunity for detailed follow-up study. It's not a core-collapse supernova, in which a massive star burns through its fuel, collapses and explodes. It's a Type Ia supernova. That means it's happening in a binary star system, where the exploding star is a white dwarf.

items.title: Parting is sweet sorrow for parakeets—but a reunion might be worse
items.desc: Losing a member of the flock can create a ripple of disruption across parakeet society. But when a missing bird returns home after a prolonged absence, feathers will fly.

items.title: Meta-compass: An on-chip toolkit for visualizing optical spectrum and polarization
items.desc: A ruler turns length into a position on a scale. A thermometer converts temperature into the height of a liquid column. In each case, a physical quantity becomes easier to read because an instrument gives it a visible reference. We wanted to bring the same idea to light, whose properties are usually measured with separate optical components and then interpreted through additional data processing.

items.title: NASA smashed into an asteroid. Now Hera has revealed a strange new world
items.desc: A European spacecraft has revealed a mysterious, crater-covered side of the asteroid Didymos as it prepares to investigate the aftermath of NASA’s historic 2022 asteroid impact. The mission could uncover new clues about the collision and help turn asteroid deflection into a powerful defense against future threats to Earth.

items.title: A mysterious twist in the universe’s oldest light could reveal new physics
items.desc: Scientists have spotted hints of a mysterious rotation in the universe’s oldest light that could reveal new physics and shed light on dark matter and dark energy. A new technique developed at UC San Diego could help rule out misleading telescope errors, bringing researchers closer to determining whether the strange signal is real.

items.title: The hidden language of psychopathy is not what scientists expected
items.desc: Scientists have discovered that psychopathic traits are associated with surprisingly different patterns of language, with some individuals using more positive words and others expressing greater negativity or less anxiety. The findings challenge familiar stereotypes about psychopathy and suggest that the stories people tell about their lives may offer important clues about their personalities.

items.title: Scientists tracked kids for 8 years. What they found about screen time was surprising
items.desc: A surprising Finnish study found that children who spent more time using screens tended to have better cognitive processing abilities as teenagers, challenging the assumption that screen time is always harmful. Researchers suggest that what children do on screens may matter more than how much time they spend using them.

items.title: A material just one atom thick reveals a strange quantum secret
items.desc: Researchers at the University of Osaka have discovered a remarkable quantum state forming at the boundary between a one-atom-thick material and a metal. They observed electrons behaving as though they were unusually heavy, including a previously unseen state created by interactions between the ultrathin layer and the copper beneath it. This first-of-its-kind observation reveals a promising new way to control exotic quantum behavior.

items.title: The secret to building Moon bases may be hiding in emergency blankets
items.desc: Scientists have turned the thin plastic used in emergency blankets into remarkably strong insulation that could help astronauts survive the Moon's extreme temperatures. Built from hundreds of stacked layers, the material withstands crushing pressure without losing its thermal protection, potentially paving the way for tougher, longer-lasting lunar habitats.

items.title: ESA’s Hera spacecraft is flying rectangles around NASA’s asteroid crash site
items.desc: Europe’s Hera spacecraft has arrived at the scene of NASA’s historic asteroid collision to uncover what really happened when a spacecraft slammed into Dimorphos in 2022. Its close-up investigation could reveal whether the impact left a crater or reshaped the asteroid entirely, providing crucial clues for protecting Earth from future threats.

items.title: NASA is offering $1 million for bold ideas to help build a Moon base
items.desc: NASA is offering $1 million in its new Moon Base Challenge, inviting U.S. students to develop innovative solutions for building humanity’s first permanent lunar outpost. From power systems to astronaut safety, their ideas could help make long-term life on the Moon possible and pave the way to Mars.

items.title: A hidden biological divide may help explain Alzheimer’s and chronic pain
items.desc: New research reveals that biological sex, genetics, and menopause may dramatically influence Alzheimer's risk, treatment responses, and chronic pain conditions such as fibromyalgia. Scientists also uncovered surprising differences in immune activity and gut-brain interactions, opening the door to more personalized treatments for neurological disorders.

items.title: Vitamin C could help block cancer-linked chemicals in your stomach, study finds
items.desc: Scientists have discovered that vitamin C may help prevent potentially cancer-causing chemicals from forming in the stomach after eating foods containing nitrates and nitrites. A new mathematical model suggests that taking vitamin C after meals could reduce these harmful reactions, offering a possible new strategy for lowering cancer risk.

items.title: Physicists defy expectations by controlling the magnetic heart of a single atom
items.desc: Scientists have unexpectedly discovered how to control the magnetic spin inside a single atom's nucleus using radio waves, overturning previous assumptions about atomic behavior. The breakthrough could pave the way for more reliable quantum memory, although researchers are still trying to understand why it works.

items.title: An ancient virus may help explain what makes the human brain different
items.desc: A virus that infected chimpanzees millions of years ago may have helped shape one of the most important differences between humans and our closest relatives: how our brains develop. Scientists at Lund University discovered that ancient viral DNA embedded in the chimpanzee genome switches off a gene called LINC00662, which remains active in humans and appears to play an important role in early brain development.

items.title: Uranus and Neptune’s bizarre magnetic fields may finally be explained
items.desc: The strange, wildly tilted magnetic fields of Uranus and Neptune have puzzled scientists since NASA's Voyager 2 spacecraft explored the planets in the 1980s. New simulations suggest that extreme conditions deep inside these icy giants create unusual electrical properties that could explain their magnetic fields. Remarkably, the models indicate that their magnetic poles could shift by tens of degrees within just a few decades, far faster than Earth's.

items.title: Astronomers discover a dead star spinning every 8 minutes and sending mysterious radio pulses
items.desc: Scientists have discovered a strange stellar pair more than 5,000 light-years away, where a dead star spinning every eight minutes produces mysterious radio pulses while orbiting a Sun-like star. The breakthrough also revealed massive magnetic storms on the companion star, offering fresh clues to one of astronomy's emerging mysteries.

items.title: Hidden ecosystem: Scientists discover 245 animals living inside a single deep-sea rock
items.desc: Deep beneath the Pacific Ocean, scientists have discovered tiny hidden ecosystems inside metal-rich rocks that take millions of years to form. Researchers examined 244 nodules and found more than 4,100 animals living in their cracks and cavities, including unique communities unlike those in the surrounding seafloor mud. These remarkable miniature habitats could now be threatened by deep-sea mining for valuable metals.

items.title: Nigeria’s Big Bet on Health Care
items.desc: Nigeria’s dependence on imported medicines and medical equipment leaves families exposed to exchange-rate fluctuations and hospitals at the mercy of global supply chains. Expanding domestic manufacturing is essential to reducing the cost of treatment and ensuring that more Nigerians can access quality care.

items.title: What Should the Nvidia Board Do?
items.desc: The proper role of any corporate board is to strike a careful balance between stakeholders. In Nvidia's case, the board will have to consider not just the current trading price, but also how its decisions will affect the landscape in which it operates, its employees, and its license to trade.

items.title: The Roots of Macron’s Failure
items.desc: Although French President Emmanuel Macron has certainly made mistakes, his troubled presidency is symptomatic of a deeper problem. In the end, he failed to build something truly enduring because he was seduced by the same monarchical impulse that is a recurring feature of French political culture.

items.title: Yalta in Shenzhen?
items.desc: In principle, the planned summit of the US, Russian, and Chinese presidents could usefully address what should be done to limit the proliferation of nuclear weapons, ensure that AI is more a force for good than harm, and end ongoing wars and prevent new ones. But principle is one thing; in practice, we are likely to see something else.

items.title: The Perverse Effects of the AI Investment Boom
items.desc: As big tech companies increasingly turn to debt markets to finance massive investments in AI data centers, they are competing for the same pools of capital as many governments. With interest rates already high and public demands for spending on the rise, the timing could hardly be worse for vulnerable economies.

items.title: Oceania’s Three Goals for COP31
items.desc: To make COP31 the “Blue COP,” delegates must recommit to keeping the 1.5° Celsius warming goal alive, reform the climate-finance system, and address our dependence on the fossil fuels driving the ocean's warming and acidification. Pacific countries have long championed these causes, but now the rest of the world must join them.

items.title: America After the Midterms
items.desc: The Democrats came out on top in the midterms by staying on message and focusing on affordability. But from voters’ perspective, there is an enormous difference between repudiating the administration and embracing the alternative.

items.title: Can Brexit Be Reversed?
items.desc: British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has called Brexit a mistake, and opinion polls show that his proposal to "go all the way" and rejoin the European Union has majority support. But Brexit was won by a movement, and only a movement can reverse it.

items.title: Portfolio Regime Change?
items.desc: Rather than assuming that traditional asset-allocation guidelines apply to current conditions, investors should position themselves for more volatility and uncertainty. The AI revolution and various structural forces mean that there is no going back to the familiar old diversification formula.

items.title: The Global Economy After the Iran War Ends
items.desc: Even if the Iran war ended tomorrow, the global economy would not simply pick up where it left off. Reopening the Strait of Hormuz could bring down commodity prices and ease inflation, but postwar reconstruction could redirect capital away from the United States, undermining the AI supercycle and fueling de-dollarization.

items.title: Breaking Billionaires’ Political Grip
items.desc: The US midterm elections showed that despite the outsize role of money in politics, even the biggest donors don’t always get their way. But defeating billionaires at the ballot box won’t stop them from buying political influence as long as the rules permit them to do so.

items.title: The Dance of Empires
items.desc: Empires have a habit of preparing to fight the last war while their rivals work out how to win the next one. The US is no different, pouring its resources into military adventures while China slowly but steadily reclaims the scientific and technological leadership that once made it the world's greatest power.

items.title: The Rare-Earth Game
items.desc: China will probably not impose a rare-earth embargo, but it will keep the specter of one alive. And the West will probably not achieve self-sufficiency in this critical sector, but it will keep seeking to reduce its vulnerability to a supply shock through expensive capacity duplication and stockpiles.

items.title: Why Research Matters
items.desc: Over the past 21 months, in the country that has leveraged research to greatest effect, the government is slashing funding for it, closing centers where it is done, politicizing grant-making decisions, and bullying its single biggest engine: universities. The costs will be far greater than many realize.

items.title: Africa Needs a Different Kind of Climate Finance
items.desc: Roughly half of the climate finance that flows to Africa comes in the form of debt, with multilateral and bilateral development-finance institutions often lending at commercial rates to economies already struggling to carry the added costs. To maximize fiscal space, the instruments used to deliver climate finance need to change.

items.title: A beginner’s guide to falling in love with Russian literature
items.desc: Few literary canons inspire as much reverence, and fear, as Russia’s. The sheer size and complexity of novels like Leo Tolstoy’s War and Peace (1867) and Fyodor Dostoevsky’s The Brothers Karamazov (1880) have created two groups of readers: Those who have read them, and those who say they will read them — one day. For one reason or another, that day never seems to come. Allow us to make the case for why it should.
